sections.report:
First read: the eye goes to the big headline "Plan the week with your whole team", then right to the white form card and the blue "Create account" button. It is a sign-up page for a team planning SaaS. It feels calm and tidy, and generic.

Job (assumed): get a new visitor to create a free Tallyboard workspace.

Walk, The whole piece:
- Purpose clear in one sentence: yes
- Image and headline make one idea: yes (no image, nothing to clash)
- Every element does a job: yes
- One mood and era: yes
- Copy finished, no placeholders or typos: yes
- Each kind of element looks the same everywhere: yes (one button, one link)
- Colors and shapes fit the mood: yes
- Headings name their section: yes

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**

None. Every checklist line is yes. The copy rules in critic.md ("The words are part of the design") have no checklist line here, but two copy findings turned up under them. I'm passing both on for the director to weigh:

1. *(No checklist line; copy, the price claim)* "Start a free workspace for up to five people. You can invite the rest of the team later." (left column, about x 140–565, y 316–362). A stranger can read this two ways. One: the workspace is free for good, but only up to five people. Two: it starts free and you pay once the team grows past five. "Invite the rest of the team later" sounds like it's still free, but the five-person cap says otherwise. The viewer can't tell if they're signing up for a free plan or the start of a paid one. This is a pricing line, so they will hold the company to whatever they took it to mean. The "Create account" button (716–1096, 549–595) doesn't say "free" either. Fix: say what happens after five people in plain words, for example "Free for up to 5 people. Paid plans start at X when you add more." Or say it's a trial if it is one. Defect. Weight: major. It's the one line that decides whether a cautious team lead signs up.
2. *(No checklist line; copy, the headline)* "Plan the week with your whole team" (140–487, 207–295) could sit on almost any team-planning or task tool's page. Nothing says what Tallyboard does differently or how it compares to what the viewer uses now (a spreadsheet, a standup, another tool). It's the biggest text on the page and gives no reason to choose this tool. Fix: name the specific thing it does, or put it next to what the team uses now. Taste. Weight: minor, because a visitor who reaches a sign-up page has usually already decided.

**What's working.**
- It reads as one piece. One typeface family, one blue used only for the wordmark and the main button, plain grey and white surfaces, and the same small corner radius throughout. Nothing feels pasted in from somewhere else, and the blue button is clearly the thing to do.
- Its purpose is clear within a couple of seconds. The wordmark, a headline about the outcome, and a card titled "Create your account" tell a first-time visitor what the page is and what to do.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The headline "Plan the week with your whole team" (about x 140–490, y 208–295) is clearly the largest, heaviest thing on the page, so the eye lands there first. The second stop is the solid blue "Create account" button (716–1096, 549–595), the only big block of saturated colour. That gives a clean path: what this is, then what to do. The headline wins on size and the button wins on colour, so they don't compete.
- The type levels are separated by more than size. The headline and the card title are bold dark text, the supporting paragraph is regular grey, field labels are small bold dark text, placeholders are lighter grey, and the "Already have an account?" line is the smallest and greyest. Each level is told apart by weight or colour as well as size, so none of them reads as an accident. The logo "Tallyboard" (about 20 px) and "Create your account" (about 22 px) are close in size, but the logo's blue and the fact that they sit in separate columns keep them from colliding.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** and **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?**
   - Where: the left column (wordmark, headline, subline) fills only about y 141–362, while the card on the right runs from y 96 to 665.
   - What the viewer sees: the lower-left quarter, about x 140–600 by y 370–800, is an empty field the height of the card. It reads as space left over when the copy ran out, not as a rest area set against something dense. The left side floats high and light, and the tall white card on the right carries the weight, so the page leans right and down. The open space is gathered, but in the wrong place: it has no shape and nothing to work against.
   - Why: visual weight comes from size and isolation, and a heavy side needs a counterweight (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). Empty space should stand in tension with the filled areas, not be what is left over (Ruder, *Typography: A Manual of Design*, "Contrasts").
   - Fix: give the left column a counterweight that reaches toward the bottom of the card. You can centre the text block vertically against the card, or better, fill the lower left with something that serves sign-up: a product glimpse, a short "what you get" list, or a customer line. That evens the weight and gives the open space a job.
   - Kind and weight: convention. Minor, since the form still does its job, but it is the main reason the page looks unfinished and templated.
2. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?**
   - Where: the "Tallyboard" wordmark (left, cap top about y 143, baseline about y 159) and the card heading "Create your account" (cap top about y 139, baseline about y 157).
   - What the viewer sees: the left column's top is clearly meant to line up with the card's first line, but the two look 2–4 px apart. The outer margins have the same kind of small miss: 140 px on the left and about 144 px on the right of the card.
   - Why: a placement that is almost aligned reads as a mistake rather than a choice (Arnheim, ch. I "Balance"). The source note that a grid break must read as deliberate is unverified in Samara.
   - Fix: measure both pairs in the live page and snap them. Put the wordmark's baseline (or cap top) on the card heading's, and make the left and right margins equal.
   - Kind and weight: defect. Minor: the offsets are small and sit about 500 px apart, so most viewers will not notice them.

**What's working.**
- Spacing inside the form shows the groups clearly. Each label sits about 8 px above its field, with about 29 px before the next label, so every label clearly belongs to its own input. The button and the sign-in line form their own closing group under a wider gap.
- The page is split into two jobs: the pitch on the left, the action inside one card on the right. The card holds exactly the sign-up group and nothing else, so it is obvious where to act.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (exact alignment with no near-misses; empty space gathered into deliberate areas; visual weight balances).

Note: Bash was refused in this session, so I couldn't run crop.mjs or entries.mjs. The image is one screen (1280×800), so I judged it from the whole image, and I read the entries for the "no" lines directly in `references/layout.md`. The pixel positions are estimates by eye, not measurements.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** The headline at about x 140–487, y 208–296 breaks as "Plan the week with / your whole team". The first line ends on "with", which pulls the phrase "with your whole team" apart. The eye stops on a dangling preposition before it gets the half of the promise that matters ("your whole team"), so the headline reads as two fragments rather than one claim. The rule follows Bringhurst's line-break etiquette, but the reference entry marks its heading-specific part as unverified, so treat this as **taste** (common sense). Fix: break at the phrase boundary, "Plan the week / with your whole team", by narrowing the headline's max-width or adding a manual break. Then check that it still breaks well at other viewport widths. **Taste, minor.**

**What's working.**
- **Clean, one-family type with a clear scale.** The page uses one sans family in about four distinct sizes, each with a plain job: the headline at about 40 px bold, the card title at about 22 px semibold, the body and input text at about 16 px, and the labels and footer at about 13 px. The steps are big enough that no size looks like a mistake. Bold labels over regular placeholders keep the two apart by weight, not by another size (Refactoring UI: bolder, not bigger).
- **The subline is set comfortably.** "Start a free workspace…" runs about 60 characters a line with generous leading, and it sits close enough under the tight two-line headline that the pair reads as one unit.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries)

**Walk (Color)**
- Small palette: yes. It uses cool grays (page #f4f5f7-ish, white card, gray input borders, gray placeholder), near-black text and one blue.
- Saturated colour kept to a small share: yes. Blue appears only on the "Tallyboard" wordmark (~140,150) and the "Create account" button (716–1096, 549–595).
- Clear light-dark range: yes. Dark headline and labels, mid-gray body and placeholders, white card on light gray. The structure holds in grayscale, and the button still reads as the darkest solid block in the form.
- Warm forward, cool recede: yes. The whole piece is cool. The CTA comes forward through saturation and value rather than temperature, and that works.
- Matching colours look the same: yes. The wordmark blue and the button blue read as the same hue, one on gray and one as a fill.
- No vibrating edges: yes. White on mid-blue is a clear lightness step.
- Status colours used only for their meaning: yes. Blue is the brand and primary-action colour, with no clash with a status meaning.
- Colour not the only carrier of meaning: yes. Nothing here relies on colour alone.
- Dark theme gray, not black: yes (not a dark theme).

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One accent, used twice and on purpose.** The single blue ties the "Tallyboard" wordmark (top left, ~140,150) to the "Create account" button (716–1096 × 549–595). In a field that is otherwise all neutral, the button is the only saturated block. The eye goes to the one action without any other help. Keep it the only saturated colour on the page.
- **Neutrals carry the structure through value.** There are near-black headings and labels, mid-gray body copy and placeholders, a white card and a light gray page. Each layer is a separate step of lightness, so the page reads the same in grayscale. Keep those steps distinct if any gray is retuned.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Walk (working notes): the only image-like element is the "Tallyboard" wordmark (blue bold text, about x140–243, y140–162). It has no photos, illustrations, or icons.
- Every image shows content: yes. Full quality: yes. Crops: yes. Figure and ground: yes. One rendering style: yes. Photo treatment: yes (there are no photos). Icon strokes: yes (there are no icons). Viewpoint and light: yes. Texture restraint: yes. No fake depth: yes (the card shadow is faint and honest). Logo clear space, undistorted, own colours: yes. Logo simple at small size and in one colour: yes.

**Section.** Pictures: applies, but only barely. The only mark is the "Tallyboard" text wordmark. There are no photos, illustrations or icons.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The "Tallyboard" wordmark (about x140–243, y140–162) has plenty of clear space around it, with at least about 45 px to the headline below and open background on the other sides. It's a single-colour set of letters, so it stays recognisable at small sizes and in one colour without any work. Its blue matches the "Create account" button, which links the brand to the main action.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 12 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. It's a signup form with five fields, a primary button and a sign-in link.

**Findings**
1. **Is everything the user needs to act visible on this screen, with nothing to remember from another?** The password rule "At least 10 characters" appears only as placeholder text in the Password field (about 716–1096, 392–436). It vanishes when the first character is typed, so a user making a password has to remember the rule while typing a hidden value. With no show/hide toggle visible, they can't check their entry against the rule either, and finding out at submit means another try (Nielsen, heuristic 6: labels and needed information belong with the field, not in a placeholder that disappears). Fix: put the rule as persistent helper text under the field, or under the "Password" label, and leave the placeholder empty or decorative. Convention. Weight: minor, since it costs one failed submit at worst, but password is the field most likely to cause one.
2. **Do input borders, control edges, and meaningful icons reach 3:1 contrast against what is next to them?** All five input borders are a pale grey-blue on the white card and look to be about 2:1, below the 3:1 that WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 requires for the boundary that identifies a field. They stay findable here only because the labels sit above them. Users with low vision or on a washed-out screen will see faint boxes, and the empty fields are what tell them where to type. Fix: darken the border until it measures at least 3:1 against white (a mid grey around #8A94A3 or darker). Measure the current border color to confirm. Convention (WCAG). Weight: minor.
3. **Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?** "Sign in" in "Already have an account? Sign in" (about 966–1008, 618) is the same grey, weight and size as the sentence around it, with no underline. It isn't marked as a link even by color, so it looks like plain text. A returning user who lands here has to guess that it's clickable, and some will start filling in the signup form instead (WCAG technique G183: a link needs 3:1 against the surrounding text plus a non-color cue such as an underline, or should be underlined by default). Fix: underline it and give it the brand blue the logo uses, or a bolder weight. Defect. Weight: major for the returning-user path, since it's that user's only way out of this screen.
4. **Are required or optional fields marked?** None of the five fields is marked required or optional. Most users will assume all five are required. "Company" is the doubtful one, because a person signing up for themselves or a side team may not have one, and they'll either invent an answer or stop (Budiu, Nielsen Norman Group, "Marking Required Fields in Forms"). Fix: put an asterisk after each required label and explain it once at the top of the form, or add "(optional)" after any optional label, likely Company. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **One clear primary action.** "Create account" is the only filled, high-contrast control on the screen, it's full width, and it sits directly under the last field. There's no doubt what to press.
- **Labels and layout.** Every field has a bold label above it, closer to its own field than to the one before. The form is one column, with only the short, related First name and Last name side by side, so the fields read straight down in order.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicators on the fields and button. The borders are already faint, so the focus ring needs to be strong (at least 2 px at 3:1).
- Whether the email field uses an email input type, and whether the password field has a show/hide control when focused.
- How error messages appear on submit, and whether the two-column layout collapses to one column on narrow screens.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 27 yes, 4 no (control looks like what it does; non-text contrast 3:1; recognition rather than recall; required or optional fields marked), 2 unsure (focus indicator; fits the width without sideways scrolling)
